profiles.name: graycrum
profiles.tagline: SHORT GAME DOING THE HEAVY LIFTING
profiles.profile: This bag lives and dies by the wedges and the save shots, because the full swing keeps wandering into traffic and the approach play is basically a surveillance camera for disasters. When it gets even a little runway, it can still post something respectable, but the round-to-round shape is volatile as hell: one start it’s scrambling like a raccoon in a chip truck, the next it’s donating balls to the property. The identity is clear though — if the irons cooperate at all, this player can survive on touch and grit instead of clean ball-striking.

profiles.name: Leroy4522
profiles.profile: This is the kind of card that makes the course look like it owes somebody money. The driver, irons, and short-game all take turns setting fire to the place, and the only real mystery is which part of the bag will be the loudest asshole on a given day. There’s enough putter noise to keep the damage from becoming completely unwatchable, but the baseline is still a whole lot of missing greens, too many doubles, and not nearly enough rescue work. When the tee ball is off, the whole operation starts looking like a hostage situation.

profiles.name: derekldavis
profiles.tagline: THE WEDGES ARE OUT FOR BLOOD
profiles.profile: This profile is a mess of brutal contact and just enough survival scraps to make you squint at it twice. The big story is how fast the tee ball and short game can torch a round; when those two go sideways together, the rest of the bag is basically carrying bricks uphill. There’s a tiny bit of evidence that the putter can stay awake while everything else is on fire, which is the only reason this isn’t full-blown freefall. Right now the card reads like a player trying to hang around with damage control instead of actual golf.
